summary: Daniel (Greek) 3 (97 verses) continues the story of faithfulness. Starting with 'Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold, whose height was sixty cubits, and its width six cubits. He set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Ba', it moves through themes of faithfulness, wisdom and calls readers toward hope.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows faithfulness lived out in second temple period. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold, whose height was sixty cubits, and its width six cubits. He set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon.
But the angel of the Lord came down into the furnace together with Azarias and his fellows, and he struck the flame of the fire out of the furnace,
Then the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the province of Babylon.

questions.question: What is happening in Daniel (Greek) 3?
questions.answer: In 97 verses, this chapter daniel (greek) 3 (97 verses) continues the story of faithfulness. starting with 'nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold, whose height was sixty cubits, and its width six cubits. he set it up in the plain of dura, in the province of ba', it moves through themes of faithfulness, wisdom and calls readers toward hope. The setting is second temple period, written to jewish community. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Daniel (Greek) and why 3 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally anonymous / tradition, addressed to jewish community around intertestamental. This chapter fits the book's purpose as jewish literature — its themes of faithfulness, wisdom build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'covenant' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Binding promise/agreement God makes with people. In this chapter, it appears in context of faithfulness. For a first-time reader: think of it as binding promise/agreement god makes with people, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through faithfulness and wisdom, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 15 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'Now if you are ready whenever you hear the sound of the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, pipe, and all kinds of music to fall down and worship the image which I have made, good; bu...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about faithfulness. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
